Behavioral capabilities

Between birth and three months the system shifts from reflex to a minimally controllable learner: quiet-alert bouts lengthen, startle is suppressed, reflexive saccades give way to nascent smooth pursuit 1, and the notorious optokinetic response (OKR) asymmetry begins to abate 2, together raising sensory SNR so prediction-error machinery has clean signals to process. Behaviorally, habituation/dishabituation paradigms already show rapid attenuation to predictable repeats with recovery to novelty, providing a direct assay of early surprise-driven model updating 3. In parallel, perceptual organization accelerates as contrast and motion sensitivity climb 4, 5, 6 and face processing pivots from global outline to internal features (eyes/mouth) 7, 8, providing a sharper representational basis for learning. Remarkably, even the youngest infants do not merely detect features–they recover stable distal-world properties from variable retinal input. Newborns (1-6 days) exhibit size constancy, responding to the real size of an object rather than its retinal projection across changes in viewing distance 9. Shape constancy is similarly present at birth: neonates habituated to a shape at one slant treat the same shape at a novel slant as familiar while treating a different shape that produces the same retinal projection as novel 10. Relatedly, preferential-looking and novelty-preference paradigms indicate that recognition memory is already present in the first months, but remains slow and attention-limited: infants require prolonged exposure (often tens of seconds) to subsequently recognize a stimulus 11. A further dimension of early abstraction is approximate numerosity: newborns discriminate large-ratio numerosities (e.g., 4 vs. 12) with continuous variables (element size, total area, density) controlled, indicating that the world model encodes set cardinality as an abstract property independent of specific perceptual features 12.

Multisensory binding comes online through temporal synchrony: intersensory redundancy pulls attention to audio-visual events 13, 14, early voice<->face 14 matching and oral<->visual shape transfer 15 align codes across senses; the infant starts treating cross-modal coincidences as labels rather than noise. This cross-modal alignment is not limited to audio-visual or mouth-based transfer: newborns can transfer haptically acquired shape information to vision (hand→\rightarroweye recognition), and by ∼\sim3 months infants can use manual exploration to discriminate material properties including weight differences, helping calibrate the visual world model with contact-grounded constraints 16, 17. Furthermore, the system begins modeling latent temporal structure immediately. Beyond simple sensory tuning, newborns demonstrate visual statistical learning, detecting violations in transitional probabilities within simple visual sequences 18, suggesting the brain is acting as a ’prediction machine’ from day one, calculating the likelihood of event BB given event AA to segment continuous visual streams.

Prediction in this period is not limited to two-dimensional gaze sequences: infants as young as 2 weeks display an integrated defensive response (head retraction, arm raising, distress) to a looming visual stimulus on a collision course, but not to receding or lateral motion 19. Subsequent work confirmed that defensive blinking is specific to optical patterns specifying collision trajectory rather than mere optical expansion 20, implying that the infant extrapolates a three-dimensional trajectory from two-dimensional optic flow and predicts contact with the self–an early form of egocentric spatial prediction. Parallel evidence from audition shows that temporal prediction is domain-general from birth. Sleeping newborns generate mismatch responses when an expected beat is omitted from a rhythmic auditory pattern, with the response time-locked to when the beat should have occurred–demonstrating generative temporal prediction over an absent event 21.

The social channel is biased from the start: newborns ( 2 days old) preferentially attend to faces displaying direct gaze over averted gaze 22, providing an attentional prior that marks moments of communicative intent and high informational value before any social reward loop is established. Social orientation and proto-communication then structure the data stream: the ≈\approx6-8-week "two-month shift" (mutual gaze (locking eyes) and the social smile 23, 24) creates a closed-loop social reward that stabilizes proto turn-taking 25, 26, while caregiver-specific recognition for voice/odor/face anchors value to people 27, 28, 29. In live interaction, infants also exhibit anticipatory postural adjustments when being picked up (2-4 months), consistent with predicting others’ imminent actions toward the self rather than purely reacting 30. By  10 weeks, infants discriminate caregivers’ basic facial affect displays (e.g., happy vs sad/angry), providing early affective labeling of socially salient states 31

Speech isn’t heard as a continuous acoustic soup: classic work shows categorical perception of speech contrasts in very young infants (including  1-month-olds), meaning the auditory front-end is already carving the space into discrete-ish partitions that later map cleanly onto phonemes/words 32. Even earlier, newborns prefer listening to their native language and discriminate languages using broad rhythmic/prosodic cues, implying early partitioning over long-timescale acoustic structure 33, 34. Vocalization shifts from reflex-dominated (cry/grunt) toward increasingly voluntary "protophones" (comfort sounds / early coo-like phonation), effectively giving the agent a controllable action channel into the social environment that can be reinforced by contingent caregiver responses 35. The model also comes equipped with an ’Animate Prior’: unrelated to face processing, newborns (1-3 days old) show a distinct preference for biological motion (point-light displays of biological kinematics) over rigid or random motion 36. This allows the infant to instantly segment the visual scene into ’Agents’ (biological dynamics) and ’Objects’ (Newtonian dynamics). Furthermore, the ’Ecological Self’ is established via proprioceptive prediction: newborns distinguish between self-touch and external-touch (rooting significantly less when their own hand touches their cheek), indicating an early form of corollary discharge that filters ’self’ from ’world’ 37. A newborn study tests statistical structure in speech (Figure) 103. The study measures neural responses to structured streams (Figure).

On the instrumental side, action-outcome contingency learning is reliable by  2-3 months (mobile-conjugate kicking, with retention extendable by reminders 38, 39, 40); even earlier, newborns can use nonnutritive sucking as an operant control variable to select auditory outcomes (e.g., different sucking patterns produce the mother’s voice versus another voice), and neonates show contingency sensitivity in high-amplitude sucking paradigms that reinforce sucking with auditory stimulation/variation 27, 41. Operant shaping is not confined to sucking: head turning can be conditioned in human newborns, demonstrating learnable orienting policies that actively sample the sensory scene 42. More generally, by 8-10 weeks infants show robust behavioral reactions to response-contingent stimulation, and by ∼\sim3 months they differentially allocate gaze/smiles as a function of social contingency (e.g., disruption vs normal vs imitation), indicating that the infant is beginning to explicitly track whether outcomes are contingent on its own actions (and others’) 43, 44. A 2025 experiment studies action–outcome contingencies (Figure) 105. The study identifies distinct movement patterns (Figure). The authors compare limb movement across ages and phases (Figure). Movement profiles are compared across connected and unconnected limbs (Figure).

Early "control" is bottlenecked by the body: improvements in head/postural control over the first months stabilize gaze and make hand-eye contingencies learnable; posture and reaching co-develop as a coupled control problem (stabilize the platform -> unlock goal-directed limb control) 45, 46. Even earlier, newborns exhibit organized hand-to-mouth coordination, and 2-day-old neonates preferentially attend to thumb-to-mouth actions specifically when anticipatory mouth opening predicts the action’s target–suggesting sensitivity to goal-structured body actions and predictive cues 47, 48. Meanwhile, spontaneous "general movements" provide rich exploratory variability–usable as motor babbling for learning sensorimotor contingencies (active system identification) 49. By the end of this window (and clearly in the 2–5 month range), nutritive sucking itself shows online adaptation to external constraints (flow/shape/flexibility of teats), highlighting early closed-loop control over a complex action sequence 50.

Overall, by the end of this window the agent can predict a bit, control a bit, and bind across senses and agents.

Training data and optimization

Training data

How to bootstrap with little-to-no priors 51

Training data in 0-3 months comes from several concurrent streams. Endogenous offline activity (REM twitches and stage-2 spindles) generates labeled sensorimotor tuples for consolidation while the infant still sleeps  14-17 hours/day 52, 53. Awake, self-initiated motor babbling produces proprioceptive, vestibular, and visual reafference, yielding dense, signed physical errors (e.g., retinal slip (eye movement errors)) that cortical and cerebellum-brainstem circuits use for supervised calibration 54, 55, 56.

Memory dynamics and offline compilation improve: habituation speeds up 57, novelty preference strengthens, sleep remains abundant ( 14-17 h/day with heavy REM) 58, and stage-2 spindles emerge over weeks 3-9 53, so REM twitches and N2 spindles (N2 = stage-two sleep (NREM)) can drive consolidation of the day’s discoveries 59.

Social contingencies (e.g infant-directed speech 60 and mutual gaze 61) provide high-SNR, quasi-labeled samples and scalar reward.

Ambient physical exafference (e.g gravity, being carried/rocked, textures, temperature, luminance transitions) supplies continuous dynamics that tune feedforward gains and gaze stabilization.

Interoceptive cycles (e.g hunger->satiety, thermal discomfort->comfort) set objectives and adjust trial-wise learning rates via neuromodulatory precision and valence.

Cross-modal temporal synchrony (e.g mouth-voice, optic-flow-acceleration, visuo-tactile co-events) acts as a self-supervised label for binding and invariances.

Circadian and ultradian schedules (e.g light/dark and feeding rhythms) entrain plasticity windows and sampling distributions.

Caregiver curation (e.g pose support, swaddling, pacing/rocking, object placement) actively shapes the exploration policy and task difficulty.

Optimization

Throughout this stage, local predictive learning in sensory cortices runs continuously: newborns exhibit mismatch responses and statistical learning even in sleep 62, 63, 64; in vision, contrast sensitivity and acuity rise steeply ( 2.4-> 4.0 cyc/deg from 1->3 months) 65, 4, motion-selective responses are detectable by  5 weeks 66, and face-selective N290/P400 components emerge by  3 months 67, 68, 69. These are textbook signatures that early sensory representations are being tuned by prediction errors. A longitudinal study tests visual statistical learning (Figure) 104. The study compares neural learning measures over time (Figure).

The cortex also helps train action: self-generated twitches during active sleep and early quiet-sleep spindles drive somatotopic bursts over S1/M1, refining body maps 70, 71.

In wake, the rapid improvement of smooth pursuit around 2 months 1 implicates cortical motion perception circuits (e.g MT/MST/FEF) learning basic target dynamics 72 while cerebellar supervised calibration refines reflexes and sensorimotor forward models from dense error streams (retinal slip, vestibular mismatch (balance)), visible behaviorally in the rapid reduction of monocular optokinetic reflex (OKR) asymmetries 2 and the early maturation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) set-point 73.

Concurrently, behavior has the operant fingerprint of cortico-basal-ganglia RL: by 2-3 months, infants in the mobile-conjugate task raise kicking when it produces the sensory reward (mobile motion), stop when the contingency is removed, and show longer retention under spaced reactivation–precisely the acquisition->extinction->retention pattern expected when a dopamine-trained striatal critic updates action values and a cortico-striatal actor adjusts policy 74, 75. Neuromodulators schedule these loops, with DA providing distributional value errors 76, 77 and ACh/NE setting precision and learning rates 78, 79, 80, so updates are strongly gated by arousal and context.

Neural development

Remarkably, there is substantial evidence indicating that high-level category-selectivity (e.g faces vs. scenes, animate vs. inanimate, object size) is already detectable in the ventrotemporal cortex by 2 months 81, 82, suggesting the cortical perceptual hierarchy comes online well before the motor hierarchy can utilize it. This recent study illustrates fig. 1 Characterizing the development of visual representations (Figure) 102. This recent study illustrates fig. 4 Global organization by animacy emerges in the ventral stream throughout the first year of life (Figure).

Neurally, the 0-3-month trajectory is a fast, lawful handoff from transient, endogenously dominated regimes to thalamo-cortically gated, externally driven ones, marked by rising oscillatory structure and conduction speed. Along with the aforementioned advancements in visual-cortical representations (contrast sensitivity, visual acuity, motion selectivity, and orientation tuning 83, 5), the ascending auditory pathway speeds up: auditory brainstem response wave latencies shorten across the first weeks to months 84, 85, indexing myelination/synchrony gains that expand temporal bandwidth for speech envelopes and fine structure 86.

This early agency operates under a ’subcortical constraint’: cortical motor outflow remains functionally disconnected from the brainstem until  3-6 months 87, meaning the infant’s earliest ’experiments’ are driven by subcortical loops that train the silent cortex–leveraging spontaneous motor babbling to build the first proprioceptive priors without top-down cortical interference.

Sleep and oscillations reorganize from neonatal "delta brushes/spindle bursts" to recognizable N2 spindles appearing at  6-8 weeks 88 and increasing through the first months 89; spindles plausibly gate plasticity at this stage, but mature SO-spindle-ripple coupling is viewed as a mature mechanism that strengthens across later infancy, childhood, and beyond 90, 91.

At the systems level, neonatal rs-fMRI already shows dynamic sensorimotor, visual, and auditory networks that reconfigure over weeks, whereas higher-order networks (e.g., DMN) are highly fragmented and strengthen later 92, 93; in parallel, myelin-sensitive MRI metrics (e.g., R1) and diffusion markers rise measurably from 0->3 months, providing the physical substrate for faster, more reliable long-range coupling across the brain 94, 95. These coordinated shifts (better SNR, faster conduction, maturing thalamo-cortical timing) directly improve the efficacy of the optimization machinery, so the same error channels operate with sharper precision and higher sample-efficiency by the end of the first quarter.

It is worth emphasizing that this stage is made possible by prenatal scaffolds. Prenatal auditory exposure seeds language priors so that, at birth, infants differentiate linguistic rhythms and can exploit infant-directed speech to drive segmentation–hence the striking efficacy of newborn statistical learning in sleep 96, 97. Subplate-mediated thalamocortical wiring peaks before birth and then reorganizes through the first months, ensuring that early sensory errors are strongly broadcast and can train cortical hierarchies once the subplate wanes 98. Fetal and neonatal REM-twitch dynamics pre-calibrate body maps and sensorimotor loops, which the cerebellum then tunes postnatally 99, 100. The prenatally-established optimization architecture (predictive coding in cortex, supervised teaching lines in cerebellum, distributional RL in BG, cortico-hippocampal loops (all gain-scheduled by neuromodulators)) means that when the world "turns on" at birth, the infant already has the right error channels and clocks; primary sensorimotor and visual networks are already functioning at birth 101. The first three months simply flood those channels with structured data: endogenous (REM/spindles) and exogenous (faces/voices/contingencies), driving rapid improvements in representation quality, control fidelity, and social learning.
